lessons.title: は and が — Topic and Subject Markers
lessons.explanation: は (wa) marks the TOPIC of a sentence (what you're talking about). が (ga) marks the GRAMMATICAL SUBJECT (the doer of the action). は sets the context; が identifies specifically who/what. This is one of the most important distinctions in Japanese.
examples: 私は学生です。(Watashi wa gakusei desu.) — I am a student. (topic)
猫がいます。(Neko ga imasu.) — There is a cat. (subject)
私は魚が好きです。(As for me, I like fish.)
誰が来ましたか？(Dare ga kimashita ka?) — Who came?
lessons.tip: Use は to talk about known/general topics; use が when identifying something new or answering 'who/what'.

quiz.question: Which particle marks the TOPIC of a Japanese sentence?
Which particle marks the grammatical SUBJECT?

lessons.title: Core Particles — を, に, で
lessons.explanation: を (wo/o): marks the direct object. に (ni): marks direction, destination, time, or indirect object. で (de): marks the place of action or means/method.
examples: 本を読みます。(I read a book.) — object
学校に行きます。(I go to school.) — direction
図書館で勉強します。(I study at the library.) — place of action
三時に起きます。(I wake up at 3 o'clock.) — time
lessons.tip: に answers 'where to?' or 'when?'; で answers 'where (action happens)?' or 'how (by what means)?'.

quiz.question: Which particle marks the direct object in Japanese?
Which particle would you use for 'at the park' (place of action)?

lessons.title: Verb Forms — Masu Form
lessons.explanation: The ます (masu) form is the polite present/future tense. It is the safest form to use in most situations. Negative: ません (masen). Past: ました (mashita). Past negative: ませんでした (masen deshita). Japanese verbs come at the END of the sentence.
examples: 食べます (tabemasu) — I eat / will eat
食べません (tabemasen) — I don't eat
食べました (tabemashita) — I ate
食べませんでした (tabemasen deshita) — I didn't eat
lessons.tip: In Japanese, the verb always comes last. Time → Place → Object → Verb.

quiz.question: What is the polite past form ending in Japanese?
Where does the verb go in a Japanese sentence?

lessons.title: Adjective Types — い and な Adjectives
lessons.explanation: Japanese has two types of adjectives. い-adjectives end in い and conjugate on their own: 大きい (big) → 大きくない (not big) → 大きかった (was big). な-adjectives need な before a noun and です for predicate: 静か (na) → 静かな公園 (quiet park) → 静かです (it is quiet).
examples: 大きい犬 (big dog) vs. 静かな図書館 (quiet library)
おいしい！(Delicious!) — i-adj.
きれいな花 (beautiful flower) — na-adj.
楽しくない (not fun) — i-adj. negative
lessons.tip: You can usually tell by looking: if the dictionary form ends in い (preceded by a Japanese syllable), it's an い-adjective.

quiz.question: How do you negate an い-adjective?
options: change い to くない

lessons.title: て-form and Connecting Verbs
lessons.explanation: The て-form connects clauses, makes requests, and forms progressive tense. て-form + います = continuous action. て-form + ください = please do. て-form + も いい = may I / it's okay to.
examples: 食べています。(Tabete imasu.) — I am eating.
ドアを開けてください。(Please open the door.)
ここに座ってもいいですか？(May I sit here?)
起きて、シャワーを浴びて、学校に行きます。(I wake up, shower, and go to school.)
lessons.tip: The て-form is one of the most versatile forms in Japanese — mastering it unlocks dozens of grammar patterns.

quiz.question: What does て-form + います express?

lessons.title: Counters — 助数詞 (Josūshi)
lessons.explanation: Japanese uses counters (助数詞) attached to numbers depending on what is being counted. 人 (people), 個 (small objects), 匹 (small animals), 冊 (bound objects like books), 枚 (flat thin objects). The number often fuses with the counter in irregular ways for 1-3, 6, 8, 10.
examples: 一人 (hitori) — one person (irregular)
二匹の猫 (ni-hiki no neko) — two cats
本を三冊買いました。(I bought three books.)
紙を一枚ください。(Please give me one sheet of paper.)
lessons.tip: Memorize counters in small groups by category (people, animals, flat objects, bound objects) rather than all at once.

quiz.question: Which counter is used for small animals like cats and dogs?
What counter is used for flat, thin objects like paper?

lessons.title: Comparison — より and 一番
lessons.explanation: To compare two things in Japanese, use A は B より (adjective) — 'A is more ___ than B.' より marks the standard of comparison. For superlatives, use 一番 (ichiban, 'most/number one') before the adjective. 方 (hō) can indicate the preferred option: A の方が B より good.
examples: 日本は中国より小さいです。(Japan is smaller than China.)
この本があの本より面白い。(This book is more interesting than that book.)
彼が一番背が高い。(He is the tallest.)
りんごの方が好きです。(I like apples better.)
lessons.tip: Remember より attaches after the thing being compared TO, not the subject.

quiz.question: Which particle marks the standard of comparison ('than')?
How do you say 'the most/number one' in Japanese comparisons?

lessons.title: Question Words and the Particle か
lessons.explanation: Japanese questions are formed by adding か to the end of a sentence, with no word-order change or verb inversion needed. Common question words include 誰 (who), 何 (what), どこ (where), いつ (when), なぜ/どうして (why), and どう (how). Question words usually stay in the same position the answer word would occupy.
examples: これは何ですか？(What is this?)
誰が来ますか？(Who is coming?)
どこに行きますか？(Where are you going?)
いつ日本に行きますか？(When are you going to Japan?)
lessons.tip: Just add か to the end of any statement to turn it into a question — no need to change word order like in English.

quiz.question: What particle turns a Japanese statement into a question?
Which word means 'where' in Japanese?

lessons.title: Conditional Forms — と, ば, たら, なら
lessons.explanation: Japanese has four main conditional forms, each with different nuances. と: natural/automatic result. ば: hypothetical condition (if and only if). たら: when/after or if (completed condition). なら: given the topic/if it is the case that.
examples: 春になると、桜が咲く。(When spring comes, cherry blossoms bloom.) — と
もっと練習すれば、上手になる。(If you practice more, you'll get better.) — ば
駅に着いたら、電話して。(When you arrive at the station, call me.) — たら
東京に行くなら、浅草がいいよ。(If you're going to Tokyo, Asakusa is good.) — なら
lessons.tip: Start with たら — it's the most versatile and natural-sounding for everyday speech.

quiz.question: Which conditional is best for 'Call me when you arrive'?

lessons.title: Potential Form — できる and -られる
lessons.explanation: The potential form expresses ability ('can do'). For する verbs, use できる. For る-verbs (ichidan), replace る with られる. For u-verbs (godan), change the final u-sound to the e-sound and add る (e.g., 話す → 話せる).
examples: 日本語が話せます。(I can speak Japanese.)
漢字が読めますか？(Can you read kanji?)
食べられる (taberareru) — can eat
運転できます。(I can drive.)
lessons.tip: In casual speech, られる is often shortened to れる (ra-nuki kotoba), e.g., 食べれる instead of 食べられる.

quiz.question: What is the potential form of 話す (to speak)?
Which verb means 'can do'/'is able to' when paired with する verbs?

lessons.title: Volitional Form — よう and おう
lessons.explanation: The volitional form expresses 'let's do' or 'I will (try to) do.' For ichidan verbs, replace る with よう. For godan verbs, change the final u-sound to the o-sound and add う. It is also used with と思う to express intention: 'I think I will...'
examples: 食べよう！(Let's eat!)
行こう。(Let's go.)
勉強しようと思います。(I'm thinking of studying.)
一緒に頑張ろう！(Let's do our best together!)
lessons.tip: Add と思う after the volitional form to soften a personal decision into 'I think I'll...'

quiz.question: What is the volitional form of 行く (to go)?
What does the volitional form + と思う express?

lessons.title: Giving and Receiving Verbs — あげる, くれる, もらう
lessons.explanation: Japanese giving/receiving verbs depend on direction and perspective. あげる: I/someone give to someone else (outward). くれる: someone gives TO me/my in-group (inward). もらう: I/someone receives from someone else. Choosing the right verb shows the speaker's viewpoint and social relationship.
examples: 私は友達にプレゼントをあげました。(I gave a present to my friend.)
友達が私にプレゼントをくれました。(My friend gave me a present.)
私は友達にプレゼントをもらいました。(I received a present from my friend.)
先生が手伝ってくれました。(The teacher helped me [as a favor].)
lessons.tip: くれる always implies the action benefits the speaker or their in-group — never use it for something you give to others.

quiz.question: Which verb is used when someone gives something TO the speaker?
Which verb expresses 'to receive'?

lessons.title: Keigo — Honorific Language
lessons.explanation: Japanese has three levels of politeness: 丁寧語 (teineigo — polite), 尊敬語 (sonkeigo — respectful, elevating others), and 謙譲語 (kenjōgo — humble, lowering yourself). Different verbs are used for each level: eat → 食べる (plain) / 召し上がる (respectful) / いただく (humble).
examples: 食べる → 召し上がる (eat, respectful)
言う → おっしゃる (say, respectful)
する → なさる (do, respectful)
もらう → いただく (receive, humble)
あげる → 差し上げる (give, humble)
lessons.tip: Use 尊敬語 when talking about superiors; use 謙譲語 when describing your own actions to superiors.

quiz.question: Which form of 'eat' do you use when respectfully describing your boss eating?

lessons.title: Passive Voice — れる/られる
lessons.explanation: The passive voice describes an action done TO the subject. For godan verbs, change the final u-sound to the a-sound and add れる. For ichidan verbs, replace る with られる. Japanese also has an 'adversity passive' expressing something unpleasant happening to the speaker, even with intransitive verbs.
examples: このパンは彼に食べられた。(This bread was eaten by him.)
雨に降られた。(I got rained on. — adversity passive)
先生に褒められました。(I was praised by the teacher.)
財布を盗まれた。(My wallet was stolen. [lit. 'I was stolen my wallet'])
lessons.tip: Watch for the adversity passive — it can be used with intransitive verbs like 降る (to rain) to show the speaker was negatively affected.

quiz.question: What is the passive form of 食べる (to eat)?
What does the 'adversity passive' express?
options: an unpleasant event affecting the speaker

lessons.title: Causative Voice — せる/させる
lessons.explanation: The causative voice expresses making or letting someone do something. For godan verbs, change the final u-sound to the a-sound and add せる. For ichidan verbs, replace る with させる. Context and particles (に vs を) distinguish 'make' (force) from 'let' (permission).
examples: 母は私に野菜を食べさせた。(My mother made me eat vegetables.)
先生は学生を早く帰らせた。(The teacher made the students go home early.)
子供を公園で遊ばせた。(I let the child play in the park.)
部下に資料を作らせます。(I will have my subordinate make the documents.)
lessons.tip: When the target has agency (like letting a child play), it often reads as 'permission'; with forceful contexts it reads as 'make/force'.

quiz.question: What is the causative form of 食べる (to eat)?
The causative voice can express which two meanings?

lessons.title: Causative-Passive Voice — させられる
lessons.explanation: The causative-passive combines causative and passive forms to express being MADE to do something unwillingly. For godan verbs, add せられる (often contracted to される) to the stem; for ichidan verbs, add させられる. It conveys reluctant compliance or being forced by someone else's will.
examples: 私は毎日野菜を食べさせられます。(I am made to eat vegetables every day [against my will].)
子供の頃、ピアノを練習させられました。(As a kid, I was made to practice piano.)
上司に残業させられた。(I was forced to work overtime by my boss.)
歌わされた。(I was made to sing. — contracted godan form)
lessons.tip: Godan verbs often contract させられる to される in casual speech, e.g., 歌わせられる → 歌わされる.

quiz.question: What does the causative-passive form express?
options: being forced to do something against one's will

quiz.question: What is the contracted casual form of a godan causative-passive verb?
